title: Federal Procurement & Acquisition Essentials
blurb: Three days on the acquisition lifecycle, FAR-grounded practice, source selection, and contract management — taught by practitioners who have built national procurement systems from the ground up.

modules.t: Day 1A — The Federal Acquisition System & Integrity
modules.d: How the FAR system is built, who holds authority, the thresholds that change the rules, and the integrity framework behind every award.
modules.body:
Why federal acquisition is different

Federal acquisition spends public money under rules designed to deliver best value while ensuring competition, transparency, fairness and integrity. Private purchasing can simply choose a preferred supplier; a federal buyer must be able to show that the process was lawful, competitive where required, and documented so that auditors, oversight bodies and disappointed offerors can see how and why the decision was made.

The regulatory architecture

The Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR), codified in Title 48 of the Code of Federal Regulations, is the primary rulebook for executive-agency acquisitions. Agencies issue supplements — the Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS), and others for agencies such as GSA, HHS and DOE — plus internal policies. Statutes underpin the system, including the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA), the Procurement Integrity Act, the Contract Disputes Act and the Small Business Act. The FAR's traditional structure moves through the lifecycle: general matters and integrity (Parts 1–5), competition and planning (Parts 6–12), acquisition methods and contract types (Parts 13–18), socio-economic programmes (Part 19 onward), and contract management (Parts 42–51), with clauses in Part 52.

Regulatory status note (2025–26). The FAR is being rewritten under the Revolutionary FAR Overhaul (RFO). Since 2025, virtually all agencies have adopted model class deviations that reorganise and simplify FAR text; formal rulemaking began in June 2026 with proposed rules covering many parts, and final rules are expected to follow. This course uses the traditional FAR part numbers, which remain the common reference, and teaches durable principles. Before acting on any specific requirement, check the current FAR, your agency's RFO deviation text and its supplement (e.g., DFARS) at acquisition.gov.

Who can bind the government

Only a contracting officer (CO) acting within the limits of a written warrant can enter into, modify or terminate contracts on behalf of the government. Programme managers, contracting officer's representatives (CORs) and technical staff cannot — however senior. When someone without authority directs a contractor to perform work, the result is an unauthorized commitment, which can only be ratified by an official with authority under defined conditions (FAR 1.602-3). Unauthorized commitments are a recurring audit finding and can leave individuals personally exposed.

Thresholds that change the process

Dollar thresholds determine which procedures apply. Following the statutory inflation adjustment effective 1 October 2025, key thresholds include: the micro-purchase threshold, raised from $10,000 to $15,000 (purchases often made by government purchase card with minimal competition); the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT), raised from $250,000 to $350,000 (streamlined procedures under Part 13); the threshold for requiring certified cost or pricing data, raised from $2 million to $2.5 million; and the ceiling for simplified procedures for commercial products and services, raised to $9 million. Thresholds are adjusted for inflation every five years and some vary for specific purposes, so always confirm current values.

Competition: the default

CICA requires full and open competition unless a statutory exception applies (FAR Part 6), such as only one responsible source, unusual and compelling urgency, international agreement, or authorisation by statute. Using an exception requires a written justification and approval (J&A) at the appropriate approval level. Competition is not a formality: it drives price, quality and innovation, and protects the integrity of public spending.

Integrity framework

The Procurement Integrity Act (FAR 3.104) prohibits knowingly disclosing or obtaining contractor bid or proposal information or source selection information before award, and governs employment discussions between officials and offerors. FAR Part 3 also addresses gratuities, kickbacks, contingent fees and personal conflicts of interest; Part 9.5 addresses organisational conflicts of interest, where a contractor's other activities could impair objectivity or give an unfair competitive advantage. Ethics rules on gifts apply to every employee involved in acquisition.

Practitioner's lens. Systems built from the ground up — in the U.S. or in national procurement reforms abroad — succeed when integrity is designed into the process: segregated roles, documented decisions, controlled information and independent review. Procedures without integrity produce paperwork; integrity without procedures produces inconsistency. Federal acquisition needs both.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my federal acquisition coach. Give me eight short scenarios involving authority (who can bind the government), thresholds, competition exceptions and procurement integrity. For each, ask what the correct action or rule is. Then explain the answer with the relevant FAR part, remind me to confirm current thresholds and any RFO deviation text, and score my performance.

📚 Glossary

  • FAR: Federal Acquisition Regulation, 48 CFR
  • Contracting officer: official with warranted authority to bind the government
  • Unauthorized commitment: agreement made by someone without authority
  • J&A: justification and approval for other than full and open competition
  • Procurement Integrity Act: prohibits improper disclosure of proposal and source selection information
  • RFO: Revolutionary FAR Overhaul (2025–26)

📖 References

  • Federal Acquisition Regulation, 48 CFR Chapter 1 — acquisition.gov.
  • FAR Council — Revolutionary FAR Overhaul model deviation text and proposed rules (2025–26), acquisition.gov.
  • Inflation adjustment of acquisition-related thresholds, effective 1 October 2025 (41 U.S.C. 1908).
  • Competition in Contracting Act of 1984; Procurement Integrity Act (41 U.S.C. 2101–2107).

quiz.q: A program manager at a civilian agency wants to hand a $40,000 software subscription to the vendor her team used at a previous job, saying the paperwork for competing it is a waste. What is the strongest reason the contracting officer pushes back?
opts: Agency policy bars buying from vendors that staff have used at earlier employers
Software subscriptions must be bought through a GSA schedule regardless of value, even for small software buys
Above the micro-purchase level the buyer must show a lawful, documented competitive process
The vendor must first be registered as a small business before any federal award
quiz.x: Public buying must be defensible: above $15,000 (micro-purchase) simplified competition and documentation are expected. Small-business status or GSA use are not prerequisites, and prior use of a vendor is not itself barred.

quiz.q: A Department of Defense buyer finds that a FAR clause and a DFARS clause both address the same data-rights topic for a weapons-support contract. How should she understand their relationship?
opts: The DFARS supplements the FAR for DoD and is applied together with it, not instead of it
She should pick whichever clause is more favourable to the government in this case
The DFARS replaces the FAR for all DoD contracts, so the FAR text can be set aside for that award
The FAR controls because statutes give it priority over every agency supplement
quiz.x: Agency supplements such as DFARS implement and supplement the FAR within Title 48; they are read together. The 'DFARS replaces FAR' view is a common misconception, and clause-picking for advantage is not permitted.

quiz.q: In October 2026 a contracting specialist in Atlanta is told a colleague's checklist cites a FAR paragraph that 'no longer looks the same' online. Given the Revolutionary FAR Overhaul, what is the most sensible next step?
opts: Keep the checklist citation because traditional part numbers are still legally binding as written
Check the current FAR text and the agency's RFO class deviation before relying on the citation
Wait for final RFO rules before acting, since deviations have no effect until then
Use the citation from the 2024 printed FAR, which remains the authoritative version
quiz.x: Agencies have adopted RFO model class deviations and rulemaking is ongoing, so text may differ from older references; verify current FAR plus the agency deviation. Deviations already have effect, so waiting is wrong.

quiz.q: During an active source selection, an evaluator receives a dinner invitation from a senior manager at one of the offerors, who says he 'just wants to talk about industry trends'. What is the best response?
opts: Accept if he pays his own share of the bill, since that removes any gift problem
Ask the other offerors whether they object before deciding whether to attend
Attend but avoid discussing the procurement, then note the dinner in his own files after award
Decline, avoid any discussion of the competition and report the contact to the contracting officer
quiz.x: Procurement Integrity Act and ethics rules make contact with offerors during a competition high-risk; declining and reporting protects the process. Paying one's own share addresses gifts but not the appearance or disclosure risk.

quiz.q: A contract specialist in Washington, D.C. realises her spouse holds a significant stock position in a company that just submitted a proposal she is assigned to evaluate. What should she do first?
opts: Continue evaluating but give that proposal a second reviewer to balance her ratings and a written note of the overlap
Sell the shares quietly and continue evaluating, since the conflict will then have ended
Tell the spouse to hold the shares until award so that no trading suspicion arises
Disclose the interest to her supervisor and ethics official and seek recusal from the evaluation
quiz.x: Financial interests of a spouse are imputed to the employee; disclosure and recusal is the standard remedy. Selling shares may help later, but continuing without disclosure leaves the evaluation tainted.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian procurement officer studying US practice asks why the FAR insists on documenting decisions that a private firm could simply make. Which explanation best reflects the course's view of federal acquisition?
opts: Documentation mainly exists to slow purchasing so that budgets are not spent too quickly
Auditors, oversight bodies and losing offerors must be able to see how and why decisions were made
Written files are needed because federal contracts cannot be enforced in court otherwise
Federal buyers are personally liable for every contract unless they keep complete files during an audit
quiz.x: Public money requires transparency and accountability so oversight and offerors can test decisions. Personal liability and enforceability are misconceptions; slowing spending is not the purpose.

quiz.q: An offeror's former employee, now working at the agency, emails a proposal manager the competitor's price from the current competition. Under the Procurement Integrity Act, what is the core problem?
opts: The email breaches agency IT policy but is otherwise acceptable if no payment is made
Former contractor staff may not work for the government for two years after leaving
Disclosing contractor bid or proposal information before award is prohibited
Price data may be shared once the contracting officer has opened all proposals
quiz.x: The Act bars knowingly disclosing or obtaining contractor bid or proposal information and source selection information before award. Timing after opening does not cure it, and it is not merely an IT issue.

quiz.q: A new contracting officer in Denver signs a $2 million services contract, but her warrant limit is $1 million. What is the most accurate assessment of the situation?
opts: She exceeded her delegated authority, so the commitment needs review and possible ratification
The contractor bears no risk since it reasonably relied on her signature
The award is valid if her supervisor signs a memorandum approving it afterwards and reports it to legal counsel
The contract is fully valid because any warranted officer can bind the government
quiz.x: Only contracting officers acting within their warrant can bind the government; commitments beyond authority are unauthorised and may be ratified under FAR 1.602-3 by an official with authority. A supervisor memo is not ratification, and contractors bear risk of dealing with someone lacking authority.

quiz.q: A US agency needs a service it believes only one firm can provide. A colleague suggests skipping documentation because 'everyone knows they are the only source'. Which statute's requirement is most directly at stake?
opts: The Competition in Contracting Act's demand for full and open competition or a justified exception
The Procurement Integrity Act's limits on post-government employment of officials
The Small Business Act's requirement to set aside every contract for small firms
The Contract Disputes Act's procedures for resolving claims after a contract is awarded and payment questions
quiz.x: CICA requires full and open competition unless an authorised exception is justified and documented (FAR Part 6). The Disputes Act and post-employment rules address other stages; set-asides are not universal.

quiz.q: A Nigerian consultant compares two US buyers: one bought $12,000 of lab supplies with a purchase card after a quick price check, the other ran a full Part 15 competition for $12,000 of the same supplies. Which judgement is most sound?
opts: Both acted correctly, as Part 15 is the default method whenever the buyer has time
The card buyer used proportionate micro-purchase procedures; the Part 15 effort wasted resources
The card buyer erred because micro-purchases must still obtain three written quotes from registered vendors
The Part 15 buyer acted correctly, because purchase cards are meant for travel rather than supplies
quiz.x: $12,000 is below the $15,000 micro-purchase threshold, so streamlined card buying with reasonable price assurance is proper; a full Part 15 competition is disproportionate. Three written quotes are not required for micro-purchases.

facts.t: General micro-purchase threshold from 1 October 2025 (was $10,000).
facts.more: Raised by the statutory five-year inflation adjustment. Some purposes carry different values, so confirm the current figure and any RFO deviation text at acquisition.gov.

facts.t: Simplified acquisition threshold from 1 October 2025 (was $250,000).
facts.more: Below it, Part 13 streamlined procedures apply. Above it, full Part 14 or Part 15 procedures generally apply unless a commercial or other exception fits.

facts.t: Title of the Code of Federal Regulations where the FAR is codified.
facts.more: Agency supplements such as DFARS sit alongside it. Since 2025 the Revolutionary FAR Overhaul has been reorganising the text through class deviations — always check the version your agency has adopted.

facts.t: Year of the Competition in Contracting Act, which made full and open competition the default.
facts.more: Exceptions (FAR Part 6), such as only one responsible source or unusual and compelling urgency, require a written justification and approval.

plaibox.title: Simulation: the eager programme manager
plaibox.intro: You are a contracting officer at a civilian agency. Score: 2 = best practice, 1 = partial, 0 = risky.
plaibox.win: Sound judgement: you protected authority, competition and integrity while still helping the mission.
plaibox.lose: Revisit who can bind the government, how ratification works, and what the Procurement Integrity Act protects.

steps.s: A programme manager tells an incumbent contractor to start extra data-migration work 'right away; paperwork later'. The contractor starts.
o: Tell the contractor to stop and route the need through you
Right — only a warranted CO binds the government; stop further exposure now.
Let it continue and issue a modification next month
This blesses an unauthorized commitment and grows the liability.
Ask the PM to email the contractor a written approval
A PM's email still carries no authority to bind the government.

steps.s: The contractor has already completed $11,000 of the work in good faith and the agency benefited.
o: Pay it from the purchase card as a micro-purchase
Splitting or disguising an unauthorized commitment is not a cure.
Document and pursue ratification under FAR 1.602-3
Correct — ratification by an authorised official under defined conditions.
Refuse payment entirely; the PM must pay
Personal exposure is possible, but ratification is the defined route to consider first.

steps.s: At lunch, an offeror's business developer asks how many proposals you received for an open competition.
o: Say it is source selection information and change the subject
Correct — protected until award under the Procurement Integrity Act.
Give a rough number, since no offeror names are shared
Even counts can be source selection information; disclosure is prohibited.
Refer the question to the programme manager to answer
Avoids answering but passes the risk to someone else instead of closing it.

steps.s: The PM wants a sole-source award to a favoured firm because 'they know us best'.
o: Agree, since their familiarity with the site reduces delivery risk
Familiarity is not a CICA exception; this invites a protest.
Ask for market research and check a Part 6 exception truly applies
Right — competition is the default; any exception needs facts and a J&A.
Compete it, but write the requirements to match that firm
Tailoring to one firm is restrictive and undermines fair competition.

modules.t: Day 1B — Requirements, Market Research & Acquisition Planning
modules.d: Defining needs well, researching the market, applying small-business rules and building an acquisition strategy.
modules.body:
Most acquisition problems start with the requirement

Unclear, overly restrictive or shifting requirements cause delays, protests, cost growth and poor performance. Experienced contracting professionals invest heavily in requirement definition with the programme office, because everything downstream — competition, evaluation, contract type and administration — depends on it.

Describing the need (FAR Part 11)

Requirements should state the government's needs in terms of functions to be performed, performance required, or essential physical characteristics, and only include restrictive provisions to the extent necessary. Three common documents: a statement of work (SOW) specifying tasks, often detailed; a performance work statement (PWS) stating required outcomes and measurable performance standards, used in performance-based acquisition (FAR 37.6) and generally preferred for services; and a statement of objectives (SOO) stating high-level objectives and inviting offerors to propose their own PWS, which encourages innovation. Brand-name or overly specific requirements restrict competition and must be justified.

Market research (FAR Part 10)

Market research is required before developing new requirements and before soliciting offers above certain levels. It identifies available commercial products and services, typical industry practices, pricing, capable sources — including small businesses — and potential risks. Techniques include requests for information (RFIs), sources sought notices, industry days, reviewing existing contracts and GSA schedules, and consulting subject-matter experts. Results must be documented and should directly inform the acquisition strategy.

Commercial first. FAR Part 12 establishes a preference for acquiring commercial products and commercial services where they meet the need, using streamlined procedures and commercial terms. Market research determines whether commercial solutions exist; unnecessary government-unique requirements increase cost and risk.

Small business and the rule of two

Federal policy requires maximum practicable opportunity for small businesses. Under the rule of two, an acquisition above the micro-purchase threshold must generally be set aside for small businesses when there is a reasonable expectation that offers will be received from at least two responsible small businesses and award will be made at fair market prices (FAR 19.502-2). Programmes for 8(a), HUBZone, service-disabled veteran-owned and women-owned small businesses have additional authorities. Market research findings support set-aside decisions, and agencies work with their small business specialists.

The independent government cost estimate

An independent government cost estimate (IGCE) estimates what the requirement should cost, prepared independently of offerors' pricing. It supports budgeting, price reasonableness determinations and evaluation of proposals. Good IGCEs document assumptions, sources (historical contracts, market data, labour rates) and methodology.

Acquisition planning (FAR Part 7)

Acquisition planning integrates the efforts of everyone responsible for an acquisition to meet the need in the most effective, economical and timely manner. Written plans typically address background and objectives, the requirement, cost, capability and performance, delivery, trade-offs, risks, competition and sources, contract type, source selection approach, budgeting and funding, management of the contract, and milestones. Planning should start early — complex acquisitions can take a year or more.

Choosing the vehicle

Options include a new standalone contract, orders under existing indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity (IDIQ) contracts, GSA Multiple Award Schedule orders (FAR 8.4), governmentwide acquisition contracts (GWACs), blanket purchase agreements, or required sources (FAR Part 8). Using existing vehicles can save months but must fit scope, ordering procedures and fair-opportunity requirements.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my acquisition planning partner. I will describe a requirement. Help me decide between SOW, PWS and SOO; draft measurable performance standards; design a market research plan (RFI questions, sources sought, industry day); assess the rule of two; outline an IGCE with assumptions; and draft an acquisition plan outline under FAR Part 7, flagging what I must confirm in current FAR and agency supplements.

📚 Glossary

  • PWS: performance work statement with outcomes and measurable standards
  • SOO: statement of objectives inviting offerors to propose solutions
  • Rule of two: set-aside requirement when two or more responsible small businesses are expected
  • IGCE: independent government cost estimate
  • IDIQ: indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract
  • Market research: collecting and analysing information about capabilities in the market

📖 References

  • FAR Parts 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 19, 37 — acquisition.gov.
  • Small Business Administration — contracting programmes and set-aside guidance.
  • GSA — Multiple Award Schedule ordering guidance.
  • OFPP — Seven Steps to Performance-Based Acquisition.

quiz.q: A Veterans Affairs office in Ohio wants janitorial services and drafts a 40-page task list saying how many times staff must mop each room. A colleague suggests restating it around cleanliness outcomes. What does the course suggest?
opts: Keep the detailed SOW because a task list makes surveillance easier and limits disputes with the cleaning contractor later
Switch to a SOO so offerors design every standard, avoiding the need to measure
Use a PWS with measurable cleanliness standards, as performance-based approaches are preferred for services
Issue the task list as a brand-name requirement to ensure a known supplier's methods
quiz.x: FAR 37.6 prefers performance-based acquisition with a PWS stating outcomes and measurable standards. A SOW is the runner-up but prescribes methods; a SOO still needs measurable standards in the resulting PWS.

quiz.q: An agency in Texas wants an innovative cybersecurity solution and is unsure how industry would approach it. Which requirement document best fits, and why?
opts: A performance work statement drafted by the agency with fixed technical methods
A detailed statement of work, so every offeror prices exactly the same tasks
A brand-name specification naming the leading product to reduce evaluation risk
A statement of objectives, letting offerors propose their own PWS and approach
quiz.x: A SOO states high-level objectives and invites offerors to propose the PWS, encouraging innovation when the approach is uncertain. A government-drafted PWS works when outcomes are well understood; a detailed SOW stifles innovation.

quiz.q: A program office insists a laptop requirement name a specific brand because 'staff like it'. Market research shows three manufacturers meet the functional needs. What should the contracting officer do?
opts: Split the buy into smaller orders below the micro-purchase level to avoid the issue
Describe functional and performance needs, or justify brand name with a documented rationale
Issue the brand-name requirement because user preference counts as an essential need
Accept the brand name as long as the solicitation adds the words 'or equal' afterwards together with salient characteristics
quiz.x: Requirements should state functions and performance; brand-name restrictions must be justified. Adding 'or equal' helps but still needs salient characteristics and justification; splitting to evade thresholds is prohibited.

quiz.q: Before buying $600,000 of geospatial analysis services, a DHS team plans to skip market research because 'we bought something similar three years ago'. Which point should the contracting officer make?
opts: Market research must be current and documented, as industry, prices and small-business sources change
Market research is optional above the SAT if a prior contract exists in the files and the same NAICS code
Old research can be reused unchanged if the previous contract had no protests
Market research is required mainly for commercial items, which these services are not
quiz.x: FAR Part 10 requires market research before developing new requirements and soliciting above certain levels, and results should reflect current conditions. Reusing an old file is a weak runner-up that misses new sources and pricing.

quiz.q: Market research for an Air Force training requirement finds several commercial e-learning platforms that meet 90% of needs with minor configuration. What does the commercial-first policy suggest?
opts: Develop a custom government-unique system since commercial products fall short by 10% of the stated needs
Proceed under Part 15 without considering commercial options, as training is a service
Consider adapting the requirement so it can be met by commercial services under FAR Part 12
Purchase the cheapest platform with a card, since commercial items avoid competition rules
quiz.x: FAR Part 12 prefers commercial products and services and encourages modifying requirements to fit commercial offerings where reasonable. Commercial items are still competed; ignoring them is contrary to policy.

quiz.q: A contracting team in Yaoundé studying US practice reviews RFI results for a $200,000 US requirement: four small firms look able to perform at reasonable prices. Under the 'rule of two', what follows?
opts: Seek a sole-source justification, since RFIs cannot substitute for formal bids
Compete it full and open, because the rule of two applies to requirements above the SAT of $350,000 under FAR Part 19
Award directly to the best small firm, as the RFI already showed its capability
Reserve the competition for small firms, as at least two are expected to offer at fair prices
quiz.x: Where there is a reasonable expectation of offers from two or more capable small businesses at fair market prices, the acquisition is set aside (FAR Part 19). An RFI is not a competition, so direct award is wrong.

quiz.q: An acquisition plan for a $25 million IT modernisation is due. Which content would most strengthen the plan for later reviewers?
opts: Linking market research findings to the chosen strategy, contract type, competition and risk approach
Copying the prior plan's narrative and changing the dates and dollar figures
Focusing on the schedule for now, since strategy can be decided during evaluation
Listing every possible contract type with neutral descriptions and no recommendation for the approving official to choose from
quiz.x: Acquisition planning (FAR Part 7) should show how market research drives strategy, competition, contract type and risk. Neutral lists or recycled text fail to show reasoning reviewers can test.

quiz.q: A program office keeps adding features to a requirement after the solicitation has been drafted, and industry questions are piling up. What is the most likely downstream effect the course warns about?
opts: Lower prices because offerors will compete harder for a larger scope and adds new features
Delays, amendments, protest risk and cost growth that stem from unstable requirements
No effect, as requirement changes after drafting are absorbed in administration
Faster award because the contracting officer can fix gaps during negotiations
quiz.x: Unclear or shifting requirements cause delays, protests and cost growth because everything downstream depends on them. Fixing gaps in negotiation is the runner-up misconception; it invites inequity and protests.

quiz.q: For a $5 million facilities maintenance PWS, a program officer writes the standard 'Contractor will respond to work orders promptly'. How should it be improved?
opts: Replace it with 'respond in accordance with industry best practice' to give flexibility
Require the contractor to propose standards after award through a separate modification once the baseline period ends
State a measurable standard, such as emergency orders answered within two hours 95% of the time
Delete the standard and rely on the COR's judgement during performance
quiz.x: PWS standards must be measurable to support QASP surveillance. 'Industry best practice' is vague, and leaving standards to post-award creates disputes.

quiz.q: An agency's market research reveals a large existing GSA schedule offering exactly the training services needed at published rates. The team must award within six weeks. Which approach is most sensible?
opts: Run a new Part 15 open competition to obtain lower prices than schedule rates across the agency's offices
Place the order with any schedule holder at listed prices without any comparison
Set aside the schedule because using an existing vehicle reduces small-business participation
Consider ordering under the schedule using FAR 8.4 procedures, competing among schedule holders
quiz.x: Existing vehicles like GSA schedules are often fastest, but FAR 8.4 still requires competition or comparison among holders and seeking price reductions where applicable. Ordering without comparison is the runner-up error.

facts.more: Set in the Small Business Act. Market research and the rule of two are how individual buys contribute to it.

facts.t: Set aside for small business when 2+ responsible small firms are expected at fair market prices.

modules.d: Choosing the right acquisition method, structuring the solicitation, and allocating risk through contract type.
modules.body:
Matching method to the requirement

The FAR provides several acquisition methods. Micro-purchases (now up to $15,000 in general) use streamlined procedures, often the government purchase card, while spreading purchases among qualified suppliers. Simplified acquisition procedures (FAR Part 13, generally up to the $350,000 SAT, and up to $9 million for qualifying commercial acquisitions under the test programme) allow quotations and simpler evaluation. Sealed bidding (Part 14) suits clear, complete specifications where award is made on price and price-related factors to the lowest responsive, responsible bidder, without discussions. Contracting by negotiation (Part 15) suits complex requirements where technical approach, past performance and other factors matter, allowing discussions and best-value trade-offs. Orders under existing vehicles (Part 8.4, IDIQs, GWACs) are often fastest.

The structure of a solicitation

Requests for proposals under Part 15 commonly follow the uniform contract format: Part I (the schedule, sections A–H, including supplies or services and prices, description or statement of work, packaging, inspection and acceptance, delivery, contract administration data and special requirements), Part II (contract clauses, section I), Part III (attachments, section J), and Part IV (representations and instructions — section K representations, section L instructions to offerors and section M evaluation factors). Sections L and M must align: offerors should be asked to submit exactly what will be evaluated. Commercial solicitations use the simplified format under FAR 12.303 and the SF 1449.

Clarity reduces protests. Ambiguous evaluation criteria, inconsistent instructions, or requirements that conflict between the PWS and section M are among the most common sources of confusion and protests. A pre-release review by legal counsel and an independent contracting colleague is one of the highest-value hours in any acquisition.

Contract types: allocating risk

Contract type (FAR Part 16) allocates cost and performance risk between government and contractor. The objective is to negotiate a type and price that give the contractor the greatest incentive for efficient and economical performance, consistent with the risk.

  • Firm-fixed-price (FFP): the contractor bears full cost risk; preferred when requirements are clear and costs can be reasonably estimated. Commercial acquisitions generally use FFP or fixed-price with economic price adjustment.
  • Fixed-price incentive and fixed-price with economic price adjustment: share risk through targets or adjust for market factors such as commodity prices.
  • Cost-reimbursement types — cost-plus-fixed-fee, cost-plus-incentive-fee, cost-plus-award-fee: the government pays allowable costs plus fee; used when uncertainties prevent reliable cost estimates. They require that the contractor's accounting system is adequate for determining costs and that appropriate government surveillance is in place, and they impose more administrative burden.
  • Time-and-materials (T&M) and labour-hour: used only when it is not possible to estimate extent or duration accurately; least preferred, requiring a determination and findings that no other type is suitable, and a ceiling price the contractor exceeds at its own risk.
  • Indefinite-delivery contracts (IDIQ, requirements, definite-quantity): used when exact quantities or timing are unknown.

The cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost system is prohibited, because it rewards contractors for increasing costs.

Choosing well

Consider requirement maturity, price competition, cost estimation reliability, technical and schedule risk, the contractor's accounting system, the government's administrative capacity, and past experience. Starting a programme with cost-reimbursement during uncertain development, then moving to fixed-price for production as risks fall, is a common pattern.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my solicitation and contract-type advisor. I will describe a requirement, its value, maturity and risks. Recommend the acquisition method and contract type with reasoning, outline sections L and M so they align, identify any FAR prerequisites (e.g., determinations and findings, accounting system adequacy, ceiling prices), and list the five most likely sources of ambiguity a pre-release review should catch.

📚 Glossary

  • Sealed bidding: award to lowest responsive, responsible bidder without discussions
  • Uniform contract format: standard sections A–M for Part 15 solicitations
  • Section L / M: instructions to offerors / evaluation factors
  • FFP: firm-fixed-price contract
  • Cost-reimbursement: payment of allowable costs plus fee
  • T&M: time-and-materials, least preferred contract type

📖 References

  • FAR Parts 12, 13, 14, 15, 16 — acquisition.gov.
  • FAR 12.303 and Standard Form 1449 — commercial solicitations.
  • DAU — Contract types and source selection resources.

quiz.q: An agency needs 5,000 identical standard office chairs, with complete specifications and several capable suppliers. Price is the only real discriminator. Which method fits best?
opts: A statement of objectives inviting suppliers to propose their own chair designs
Sealed bidding under Part 14, awarding to the lowest responsive, responsible bidder
A sole-source award to the incumbent to avoid the cost of a competition
Negotiation under Part 15 with a best-value trade-off and technical discussions on each bid
quiz.x: Sealed bidding suits clear, complete specifications with award on price and price-related factors, without discussions. Part 15 is the runner-up but adds unnecessary complexity.

quiz.q: A US Army office plans a $290,000 commercial equipment purchase. Using the thresholds effective 1 October 2025, which procedure is generally available?
opts: Certified cost or pricing data procedures, since the value exceeds $250,000
Mandatory sealed bidding, since equipment purchases above $250,000 require it for durable goods
Micro-purchase procedures, since commercial items have no dollar ceiling
Simplified acquisition procedures, since the value is below the $350,000 threshold
quiz.x: The SAT is $350,000 from 1 October 2025, so $290,000 qualifies for Part 13 procedures. $250,000 was the old SAT; the micro-purchase limit is $15,000; certified cost or pricing data applies from $2.5 million.

quiz.q: A contracting officer is reviewing a draft RFP. Section L asks for a 30-page technical narrative and a staffing plan, but section M evaluates only technical approach and price. What is the problem?
opts: L and M are misaligned, since offerors are asked for content that will not be evaluated
Section M must list every page limit stated in section L to be enforceable and evaluated as a factor
Staffing plans belong in section K representations rather than in section L
Section L should be removed, since section M alone tells offerors what to submit
quiz.x: Sections L and M must align: offerors should submit exactly what will be evaluated. Misalignment is a common source of protests; removing L or moving content to K misunderstands the format.

quiz.q: A complex systems-integration requirement has uncertain scope and costs that cannot yet be estimated reliably. Which contract type is most suitable for the initial phase?
opts: A time-and-materials contract with no ceiling, to allow flexibility in labour mix
A fixed-price contract with economic price adjustment tied to inflation indices
A cost-reimbursement contract, with an adequate accounting system and active oversight
A firm-fixed-price contract, so the government transfers all cost risk immediately at contract award
quiz.x: When costs cannot be estimated with reasonable accuracy, cost-reimbursement types fit, provided the contractor has an adequate accounting system and the government monitors. FFP is the runner-up but places unreasonable risk and inflates prices; T&M must have a ceiling.

quiz.q: A contractor in Virginia proposes a $3.1 million sole-source modification for which no adequate price competition exists and no exception applies. What pricing requirement is most likely triggered?
opts: Certified data needed if the contractor is a large business under its NAICS code
A simple price analysis using catalogue prices, since the value is below $5 million
Certified cost or pricing data, since the action exceeds the $2.5 million threshold
No pricing data at all, because modifications are exempt from the requirement for this contractor
quiz.x: From 1 October 2025 the threshold for certified cost or pricing data is $2.5 million; absent an exception such as adequate competition or commercial items, it applies to modifications too. Size status is not the test.

quiz.q: A buyer wants to procure IT help desk services quickly, and the agency already has a multiple-award IDIQ covering them. What is the most important step when placing the order?
opts: Provide each awardee a fair opportunity to be considered, unless an exception is documented
Award to the awardee with the lowest overall contract ceiling for maximum savings
Choose the awardee most familiar to staff, since all awardees were pre-competed
Run a new full and open competition, since IDIQ orders cannot be competed internally for this order
quiz.x: Orders over the micro-purchase threshold under multiple-award contracts require fair opportunity under FAR 16.505, with documented exceptions. Pre-competition at the IDIQ level does not permit choosing by familiarity.

quiz.q: For a $9 million research effort, the government wants to motivate a contractor to beat cost targets and share savings. Which contract type is designed for that?
opts: A time-and-materials contract with a ceiling price and fixed hourly rates
A cost-plus-incentive-fee contract with a target cost and a share ratio
A firm-fixed-price contract with a bonus clause for completing the work early
A cost-plus-fixed-fee contract, because the fee stays the same regardless of cost
quiz.x: CPIF adjusts fee by a formula comparing actual to target cost, rewarding cost control. CPFF has no cost incentive; T&M offers the weakest cost-control incentive.

quiz.q: A small agency needs 200 laptops at about $1,200 each. A staff member proposes buying them in sixteen separate card purchases of $14,000 each. What is wrong with this plan?
opts: The plan needs approval from the small business specialist but is otherwise sound
Card purchases may not exceed $10,000 each, whatever of the item being bought
The plan is fine because each order is below the $15,000 micro-purchase threshold
Splitting a requirement to stay under the micro-purchase threshold is prohibited
quiz.x: The total is about $240,000; splitting requirements to avoid thresholds is prohibited, so simplified acquisition procedures apply. The $10,000 figure is an outdated threshold.

quiz.q: An agency wants to buy a commercial software solution worth $6 million quickly. Which approach may be available under the simplified procedures test programme?
opts: Micro-purchase procedures, since commercial software is exempt from dollar thresholds
Sealed bidding, since commercial software must be bought on price alone
Simplified procedures are unavailable because the value is above the SAT of $350,000 for this buy
Simplified procedures for qualifying commercial acquisitions up to the programme's higher limit
quiz.x: The commercial test programme allows simplified procedures for qualifying commercial acquisitions up to $9 million per the lesson (check current status). Saying the SAT bars it ignores this programme.

quiz.q: A US contracting officer must choose between FFP and T&M for a short, well-defined website redesign with stable requirements. Which choice is best and why?
opts: Time-and-materials, because labour-hour flexibility gives the government lower risk for a short project
Firm-fixed-price, because requirements are clear enough for the contractor to price the risk
Time-and-materials, because FFP contracts require certified cost or pricing data
Cost-plus-fixed-fee, because it limits the contractor's profit to a set amount
quiz.x: FFP fits well-defined requirements and gives the strongest incentive to control cost; T&M is used only when no other type is suitable and needs a ceiling and close oversight.

facts.t: Ceiling for simplified procedures for qualifying commercial acquisitions from 1 Oct 2025.
facts.more: Raised by the 2025 inflation adjustment. Check whether the authority and value apply under your agency's current FAR and RFO deviations.

facts.t: Sections of the uniform contract format used for Part 15 solicitations.
facts.more: Section L (instructions) and Section M (evaluation factors) must align: ask offerors for exactly what you will evaluate. Commercial buys use the SF 1449 format instead.

facts.t: Cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost contracting.
facts.more: It rewards contractors for increasing costs. Cost-reimbursement types instead pay allowable cost plus a fee that does not grow with cost.

facts.t: Least preferred contract type — needs a D&F and a ceiling price.
facts.more: Use only when extent or duration cannot be estimated. The contractor exceeds the ceiling at its own risk.

segments: Section C: the contractor shall deliver monthly dashboards meeting the PWS accuracy standards.
Section L: offerors shall submit a technical volume, past performance and price.
Section M: technical approach is significantly more important than past performance,
and offerors' staff diversity programmes will also be scored.

Only offerors using BrandX Analytics software will be considered.

modules.d: Trade-off and LPTA, ratings and documentation, discussions, price and cost analysis, debriefings and protests.
modules.body:
Best value has two main routes

Under FAR Part 15, the government seeks the best value. Two approaches dominate. In the trade-off process, the government may award to other than the lowest-priced offeror or the highest technically rated offeror if the perceived benefits of a higher-priced proposal merit the additional cost — but the trade-off must be documented with a rationale. In the lowest price technically acceptable (LPTA) process, proposals are evaluated as acceptable or unacceptable against non-price factors, and award goes to the lowest-priced acceptable offeror; no trade-offs are permitted. LPTA suits well-defined requirements where higher performance has little value; statutory and policy restrictions limit its use for complex services, especially in defence.

Evaluation factors and the solicitation promise

Evaluation must follow the factors and their relative importance stated in the solicitation — section M is a promise to offerors. Price must always be evaluated; past performance is generally required for negotiated competitive acquisitions above the SAT unless documented as inappropriate; quality factors such as technical approach and management capability follow the requirement. Evaluators must apply ratings consistently, document strengths, weaknesses, significant weaknesses and deficiencies, and avoid using unstated criteria.

The documentation test. Could an independent reviewer — a GAO attorney or a judge — read the evaluation record and understand exactly why each proposal received its rating and why the award decision was made? Adjectival ratings alone ("Good", "Acceptable") are not enough; the narrative must explain the underlying findings and the trade-off reasoning. Most sustained protests involve inadequately documented or inconsistent evaluations.

Clarifications, competitive range and discussions

Clarifications (FAR 15.306(a)) are limited exchanges when award without discussions is contemplated — for example, resolving minor clerical errors or clarifying past performance information — and may not be used to cure deficiencies or materially revise a proposal. If discussions are needed, the CO establishes a competitive range of the most highly rated proposals, then holds discussions with each offeror in it, which must be meaningful: addressing deficiencies, significant weaknesses and adverse past performance information the offeror has not had a chance to address. Discussions are followed by final proposal revisions.

Price and cost analysis

The CO must determine that the price is fair and reasonable. Price analysis evaluates the price without evaluating its separate cost elements — comparing competing offers, prior prices, published price lists, the IGCE or parametric estimates; adequate price competition is usually the strongest basis. Cost analysis reviews individual cost elements and profit, required when certified cost or pricing data are obtained (generally above the $2.5 million threshold where no exception applies, such as adequate competition or commercial items). Cost realism analysis is required for cost-reimbursement contracts to determine the probable cost of performance and may be used in fixed-price competitions to assess understanding or risk.

Responsibility

Award may go only to a responsible prospective contractor (FAR Part 9): adequate financial resources, ability to meet delivery, satisfactory performance and integrity record, necessary organisation and controls, and eligibility. CO checks include the System for Award Management (SAM) exclusions and performance information systems. For small businesses, a non-responsibility determination is referred to the SBA for a Certificate of Competency decision.

Debriefings and protests

Unsuccessful offerors in Part 15 competitions may request a debriefing; a post-award debriefing request must generally be received within three days of notification of award. Debriefings explain significant weaknesses and deficiencies, the overall ratings and price of the awardee and the debriefed offeror, and the rationale for award — without revealing other offerors' confidential information. Good debriefings reduce protests. Bid protests may be filed with the agency, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) or the U.S. Court of Federal Claims. At GAO, protests of solicitation improprieties must generally be filed before the closing date; other protests generally within ten days of when the basis is known, with special timing rules after required debriefings. Timely GAO protests can trigger an automatic stay of award or performance under CICA.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my source selection reviewer. I will paste anonymised evaluation narratives and a draft award decision. Check whether ratings are supported by documented strengths and weaknesses, whether unstated criteria were used, whether the trade-off rationale is adequate, whether exchanges were clarifications or discussions, and whether price analysis supports fair and reasonable pricing. List the protest vulnerabilities and how to fix each.

📚 Glossary

  • Trade-off: award to other than lowest price or highest rated with documented rationale
  • LPTA: lowest price technically acceptable
  • Deficiency: material failure to meet a requirement
  • Competitive range: most highly rated proposals selected for discussions
  • Price analysis / cost analysis: evaluating total price / evaluating cost elements
  • Responsibility: capability and integrity to perform, assessed before award

📖 References

  • FAR Parts 9, 15 (15.101, 15.306, 15.404, 15.505–15.506) — acquisition.gov.
  • GAO Bid Protest Regulations, 4 CFR Part 21; GAO Bid Protest Annual Reports.
  • U.S. Court of Federal Claims — bid protest jurisdiction (28 U.S.C. 1491(b)).
  • DoD Source Selection Procedures (current edition).

quiz.q: An agency is buying routine grounds-keeping where higher technical quality brings little added value. Which source selection approach fits best?
opts: A sole-source award to the incumbent, since its performance is already known
Sealed bidding with a technical trade-off and discussions with all bidders
Lowest price technically acceptable, awarding to the cheapest acceptable offeror
A trade-off process, letting evaluators pay more for superior technical approaches
quiz.x: LPTA suits well-defined requirements where higher performance has little value. A trade-off is defensible but adds effort and cost for little benefit; sealed bidding does not allow discussions.

quiz.q: In a trade-off source selection, Offeror A is rated Outstanding at $4.8M and Offeror B Good at $4.2M. The SSA picks A. What must the decision record show?
opts: Why A's specific benefits justify the $600,000 premium, based on documented findings
That B's price was unreasonable, since a lower-rated offer cannot otherwise lose
That A had the highest adjectival rating, which itself justifies any price difference
That A was selected because Outstanding ratings require award under the RFP
quiz.x: A trade-off must document why perceived benefits merit the extra cost. Adjectival ratings alone are not enough; B need not be unreasonable to lose.

quiz.q: An evaluator rates a proposal 'Acceptable' for management approach but writes no narrative. Why would a GAO attorney likely criticise this?
opts: GAO criticises ratings mainly when the offeror's price is also unreasonable
The record must explain the underlying strengths, weaknesses and reasoning, not just a label
The evaluator should have used numerical scores, which GAO requires for all factors
Adjectival ratings are not permitted in federal source selections issued after the 2025 policy changes
quiz.x: The documentation test: an independent reviewer must understand why each rating was given. Adjectival ratings are allowed but need narrative support; numerical scores are not required.

quiz.q: Halfway through evaluation, the panel decides 'cybersecurity certifications' should matter a lot, though section M does not mention them. What should the contracting officer do?
opts: Record the factor in the file so that its use is documented if challenged
Use the factor purely to break ties, since it was not formally stated in section M
Amend the solicitation if the factor matters and allow revised proposals, or not use it
Allow evaluators to weigh certifications informally as part of technical approach without amending the RFP
quiz.x: Section M is a promise; unstated criteria cannot be applied. Amending and allowing revised proposals keeps fairness. Documenting it does not cure the use of an unstated criterion.

quiz.q: During discussions in a Part 15 competition, a contracting officer tells Offeror X that its price is 20% above the others but does not tell Offeror Y about a significant weakness in its proposal. What is the likely issue?
opts: Discussions must be meaningful and fair, so Y's significant weakness should also have been raised
Discussions are optional, so the officer may choose which offeror to help
Revealing X's relative price position is improper, but omitting Y's weakness is acceptable under FAR 15.306 discussion rules
There is no issue, since price is routinely discussed while weaknesses are confidential
quiz.x: When discussions are held they must be meaningful, addressing deficiencies and significant weaknesses for each offeror in the competitive range, and must not favour one. Discussing price position is permitted in general terms.

quiz.q: A disappointed offeror in a $40 million award requests a debriefing. What should the debriefing generally include?
opts: A copy of the winning offeror's full technical proposal so it can compare approaches
The winner's name alone, since evaluation details are protected source selection data
Detailed point-by-point comparisons with every other offeror's confidential data in ranked order
The agency's evaluation of its significant weaknesses, overall ratings and the award rationale
quiz.x: Debriefings explain the offeror's significant weaknesses or deficiencies, overall evaluated cost/price and ratings, and the rationale for award, without revealing other offerors' proprietary information.

quiz.q: A negotiated competitive acquisition for $2 million in engineering services omits past performance from evaluation without explanation. What is the problem?
opts: Past performance is optional for services, but must be included for supplies
Past performance is generally required above the SAT unless the file documents why it is inappropriate
The omission is fine as long as price is evaluated, since price alone is mandatory
Past performance may be evaluated in LPTA acquisitions, but is optional in trade-offs where price competition is weak
quiz.x: The lesson states past performance is generally required for negotiated competitive acquisitions above the SAT unless documented as inappropriate. Price is mandatory but not sufficient.

quiz.q: An evaluation team rates two proposals with nearly identical staffing plans differently: one 'Strength', one 'Weakness'. Which risk is greatest?
opts: A protest alleging unequal treatment, because ratings were inconsistent across similar content
No risk, since evaluators may use judgement differently for each proposal on a panel that has reached consensus
A risk mainly if the higher-rated proposal also has the lower price
Mainly delay, because GAO does not review technical ratings in detail
quiz.x: Consistent application of ratings is essential; most sustained protests involve inconsistent or poorly documented evaluations. Evaluator discretion does not cover disparate treatment.

quiz.q: Under LPTA, Offeror P's technical proposal is clearly superior to Offeror Q's, but both are acceptable and Q is $50,000 cheaper. To whom should award go?
opts: P, if the contracting officer documents a short trade-off rationale in the file
Neither, since LPTA requires discussions whenever technical quality differs
P, because the government should obtain the best technical approach available given the clear superiority
Q, because LPTA awards to the lowest-priced acceptable offeror without trade-offs
quiz.x: Under LPTA no trade-offs are permitted: the lowest-priced technically acceptable offer wins. Documenting a trade-off would contradict the stated method.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian evaluator advising a US-funded project asks why US practice puts so much weight on the evaluation record. Which explanation is best?
opts: The record is mainly a training tool for new evaluators on later procurements
GAO decides protests by re-evaluating proposals itself rather than reading records
Sustained protests usually turn on poorly documented or inconsistent evaluations
Records are needed mainly when the lowest-priced offer does not win the award
quiz.x: GAO reviews the record to decide whether the evaluation was reasonable and consistent with the solicitation; most sustained protests involve inadequate documentation. GAO does not re-evaluate proposals itself.

facts.t: Time to request a post-award debriefing after notice of award.
facts.more: Requests must generally be received within three days. Good debriefings explain weaknesses, ratings and rationale — and reduce protests.

facts.t: General GAO protest deadline after the basis is known.
facts.more: Solicitation improprieties must generally be protested before closing; special timing applies after required debriefings. Timely protests can trigger a CICA stay.

facts.t: Time GAO generally has to decide a bid protest.
facts.more: Set by CICA. Agencies can also face protests at the Court of Federal Claims, which has no such statutory clock.

facts.t: Threshold for requiring certified cost or pricing data from 1 Oct 2025 (was $2M).
facts.more: Exceptions include adequate price competition and commercial products or services. Without certified data, price analysis is usually the basis for fair and reasonable.

plaibox.title: Simulation: trade-off under pressure
plaibox.intro: You are the CO on a $6M services competition. Score: 2 = best, 1 = partial, 0 = risky.
plaibox.win: Protest-resistant work: you followed Section M, kept exchanges lawful and documented the rationale.
plaibox.lose: Review clarifications vs discussions, LPTA vs trade-off, and the documentation test.

steps.s: The lowest-priced offer has a material staffing deficiency; award without discussions was planned.
o: Ask only that offeror to fix the deficiency it has
Curing a deficiency with one offeror is unequal discussions.
Award to it anyway, since price is what matters most
Under trade-off, a deficient proposal cannot simply win on price.
Decide whether to open discussions with a competitive range
Correct — deficiencies can only be addressed through discussions.

steps.s: The programme office wants LPTA to save time on this complex cyber-security service.
o: Agree; LPTA is faster and easier to defend in protests
LPTA is restricted for complex services where higher performance has value.
Keep trade-off since higher capability has real value here
Right — LPTA suits well-defined needs where extra performance has little value.
Use LPTA but add a bonus for strong résumés
