steps.s: The SSA's draft decision says only: 'Offeror C provides best value.'
o: Ask the SSA to document why C's benefits merit its price
The trade-off rationale must be explicit and traceable to the evaluation.
Attach the full adjectival rating table as support
Ratings alone are not enough; the reasoning must be written.
Accept it; SSA judgement is discretionary by rule
Discretion still must be documented — this is a classic sustained-protest finding.

steps.s: An unsuccessful offeror requests a debriefing two days after award notice and asks for the winner's labour rates.
o: Debrief, giving the awardee's overall price but not its rates
Correct — overall price and ratings are shared; confidential details are not.
Decline; the request arrived after the deadline
Two days is within the three-day window.
Send the full winning proposal so the process is transparent
Transparency is good, but proprietary data must never be released.

modules.d: Surveillance, changes, performance evaluation, payment, disputes, terminations and closeout.
modules.body:
Award is the beginning, not the end

Value is delivered — or lost — during performance. Contract administration ensures the government receives what it paid for, on time and within cost, while treating the contractor fairly under the contract terms. Poor administration produces cost growth, disputes and audit findings even after excellent source selections.

Roles in administration

The contracting officer retains authority over the contract. A contracting officer's representative (COR), designated in writing, performs technical monitoring: observing performance, inspecting deliverables, reviewing invoices for technical acceptance and documenting issues. The COR's designation letter defines limits — CORs cannot change price, quantity, delivery, scope or other terms. Programme staff should channel any desired change through the CO. A kickoff (post-award) conference aligns expectations on roles, communication, deliverables and invoicing.

Surveillance and quality assurance

For performance-based contracts, a quality assurance surveillance plan (QASP) describes how the government will monitor performance against the PWS standards — methods (100% inspection, random sampling, periodic inspection, customer feedback), frequency, acceptable quality levels and documentation. Inspection and acceptance follow the contract clauses (FAR Part 46). Acceptance generally becomes conclusive except for latent defects, fraud, gross mistakes amounting to fraud, or as otherwise provided by warranties.

Document as you go. Contemporaneous records — surveillance reports, correspondence, meeting minutes, deliverable reviews — are the government's evidence in disputes and performance evaluations. Problems discovered but not documented are almost impossible to act on later.

Modifications

Contract modifications (FAR Part 43) are written changes. Bilateral modifications (supplemental agreements) are signed by both parties — for example negotiated equitable adjustments or agreed changes. Unilateral modifications are signed by the CO alone — administrative changes, change orders under the Changes clause, and exercise of options. The Changes clause lets the CO order changes within the general scope of the contract; the contractor must proceed and is entitled to an equitable adjustment in price or schedule if the change affects cost or time. Changes outside the general scope — a cardinal change — are new work requiring competition or a justification.

A constructive change occurs when the government, without a formal change order, requires work beyond the contract — through informal direction, defective specifications, or overly strict interpretation. Constructive changes often arise from CORs or programme staff directing work, and can generate claims.

Options

Options may be exercised only in accordance with their terms, within the time specified, when funds are available, the need continues and exercise is the most advantageous method of fulfilling the requirement, considering price and other factors (FAR 17.207).

Performance evaluation and payment

Agencies record past performance in the Contractor Performance Assessment Reporting System (CPARS), evaluating quality, schedule, cost control, management, small business subcontracting and regulatory compliance. Evaluations must be accurate, evidence-based and timely; contractors may comment. Under the Prompt Payment Act, agencies generally must pay proper invoices within specified periods (commonly 30 days) or pay interest penalties.

Disputes, terminations and closeout

The Contract Disputes Act governs claims: contractor claims are submitted to the CO, and claims over $100,000 require certification; the CO issues a final decision, which may be appealed to a board of contract appeals or the Court of Federal Claims. Contracts may be terminated for convenience (government's right, with settlement of costs and reasonable profit on work performed) or for default (contractor failure, typically preceded by a cure notice for many failures). Closeout (FAR 4.804) confirms delivery, final payment, release of claims, de-obligation of excess funds and file completion.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my contract administration advisor. I will describe a performance situation (anonymised). Determine whether it involves a change within scope, a cardinal change, a constructive change or an unauthorized commitment; identify the correct modification type; outline the equitable adjustment considerations; state what must be documented; and draft a short, professional letter from the contracting officer to the contractor.

📚 Glossary

  • COR: contracting officer's representative for technical monitoring
  • QASP: quality assurance surveillance plan
  • Bilateral / unilateral modification: signed by both parties / by CO alone
  • Equitable adjustment: fair adjustment of price or schedule for a change
  • Constructive change: informal government action requiring extra work
  • CPARS: Contractor Performance Assessment Reporting System

📖 References

  • FAR Parts 4 (4.804), 17 (17.207), 33, 42, 43, 46, 49, and clause 52.243 (Changes) — acquisition.gov.
  • Contract Disputes Act (41 U.S.C. 7101–7109).
  • Prompt Payment Act (31 U.S.C. 3901–3907).
  • CPARS — guidance for assessing officials.

quiz.q: A COR at a Seattle federal office tells the contractor to add two extra training sessions 'since you're already on site', without contacting the contracting officer. What is the main issue?
opts: The change is valid if the COR records it in the next surveillance report
The change is fine if it costs less than the micro-purchase threshold
The COR lacks authority to change scope; changes must go through the contracting officer
The contractor must perform it because CORs can direct technical work for the contract file
quiz.x: CORs cannot change price, quantity, delivery or scope; such directions risk constructive changes and unauthorised commitments. Documenting it does not create authority.

quiz.q: A janitorial PWS requires 95% of rooms to meet cleanliness standards. Monthly random sampling finds 88%. According to a typical QASP, what should happen next?
opts: Document the shortfall and follow the contract's remedies, such as corrective action requests
Reduce the payment informally by 7% without notifying the contracting officer
Accept the work without comment, since 88% is close to the standard on the next invoice
Terminate the contract for default immediately because the standard was missed
quiz.x: The QASP defines acceptable quality levels and documentation; shortfalls trigger documented remedies within the contract. Immediate default termination is disproportionate.

quiz.q: After accepting a delivered generator, an agency discovers six months later that the contractor concealed a known defect. Can the government still act?
opts: No, unless the defect was noted on the receiving report at delivery
No, because acceptance is final once the inspection report is signed
Yes, but solely if the warranty clause expressly mentions generators
Yes, because acceptance is not conclusive for latent defects or fraud
quiz.x: Under FAR Part 46, acceptance is conclusive except for latent defects, fraud, gross mistakes amounting to fraud, or warranty provisions.

quiz.q: A contractor submits a written claim for $150,000 in extra costs under the Contract Disputes Act. What must the claim include at this value?
opts: A request for mediation before the contracting officer can consider it
A certification, since claims over $100,000 must be certified by the contractor
Nothing extra, as certification is required for claims above $2.5 million, like cost or pricing data
Approval from the COR, who decides claims under $500,000
quiz.x: Under the Contract Disputes Act, claims over $100,000 must be certified. The $2.5M figure is the certified cost or pricing data threshold, not the claim certification threshold.

quiz.q: An agency wants to add a new building to an existing maintenance contract, which was competed for one building only. What is the key concern?
opts: The addition may be out of scope and require a new competition or justification
The COR can add the building through a technical direction letter
The contractor can refuse, but if it agrees no further action is needed
Any change is allowed as long as the price is reasonable and funds exist for the added building
quiz.x: Changes beyond the scope of the original competition are cardinal or out-of-scope and require competition or a justification under CICA.

quiz.q: A contractor is consistently late on deliverables. Before considering default termination, what should a contracting officer usually do?
opts: Ask the COR to replace the contractor's project manager directly
Withhold all payments indefinitely until the contractor improves performance as an alternative
Issue a cure notice or show-cause notice, giving the contractor a chance to respond
Terminate for convenience at once, since it avoids any dispute
quiz.x: Default termination usually follows cure or show-cause notices documenting the failure. Termination for convenience is a different remedy; withholding payments must follow contract terms.

quiz.q: An agency closes a contract and must complete a performance evaluation. What is the main purpose of entering a CPARS assessment?
opts: To grade the COR's performance for annual personnel appraisals
To publish the contractor's rating on a public website for citizens at the end of the contract
To decide the contractor's final payment and any contract adjustments
To provide past-performance information used in future source selections
quiz.x: CPARS records feed past-performance evaluations in future competitions. They are not public and are not the basis for payment.

quiz.q: A COR approves invoices without checking deliverables because 'the contractor has always been reliable'. What risk does this create?
opts: Delaying payment beyond prompt-payment deadlines and incurring interest
Paying for work not received and weakening the government's position in disputes
A minor procedural lapse, since invoices are approved by the CO anyway for a reliable contractor
No risk if the contractor's past CPARS ratings were all excellent
quiz.x: The COR verifies technical acceptance; skipping checks risks paying for nonconforming work and losing evidence for disputes. Reliance on past ratings does not replace inspection.

quiz.q: Halfway through a fixed-price contract, the government directs a design change that increases the contractor's costs by $80,000. What is the contractor generally entitled to?
opts: Automatic conversion of the contract to cost-reimbursement for the remainder
Nothing, because firm-fixed-price contracts place all cost risk on the contractor
An equitable adjustment in price or schedule under the changes clause
A claim solely if the change was issued in writing by the COR
quiz.x: Government-directed changes within scope entitle the contractor to equitable adjustment under the changes clause. FFP risk covers the contractor's own costs, not government-ordered changes.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian ministry official studying US practice wants to know why the course stresses contemporaneous documentation during performance. Which explanation is best?
opts: Just records signed by the contracting officer have legal value later
Records made at the time are the government's evidence in disputes and evaluations
Records are mainly needed to calculate the contractor's profit at closeout for audit purposes
Documentation is optional unless the contractor files a formal claim
quiz.x: Contemporaneous surveillance reports, correspondence and minutes are the evidence in disputes and performance evaluations; problems not documented are hard to act on later.

facts.t: Contractor claims above this amount must be certified under the Contract Disputes Act.
facts.more: Claims go to the CO for a final decision, appealable to a board of contract appeals or the Court of Federal Claims.

facts.t: Common payment period for a proper invoice under the Prompt Payment Act.
facts.more: Late payment triggers interest penalties. COR technical acceptance should therefore be timely and documented.

facts.t: The system where agencies record contractor past performance.
facts.more: Assessments cover quality, schedule, cost control, management, small-business subcontracting and regulatory compliance. Contractors may comment — so evidence matters.

facts.t: FAR part governing contract modifications.
facts.more: Bilateral modifications are signed by both parties; unilateral ones (change orders, administrative changes, option exercises) by the CO alone.

labs.title: What kind of change is this?
labs.intro: Classify each event on a facilities-support contract.
items: CO issues a written order to switch cleaning products within the PWS
CO orders additional night shifts for the same buildings
COR insists on inspection standards stricter than the contract
Defective drawings force the contractor to redo work
Agency adds construction of a new warehouse to the cleaning contract
Programme analyst emails the contractor to start a new IT project
Facility manager without a warrant signs a purchase for extra security guards
labs.tip: Within scope → change order; informal direction → constructive change; outside scope → new competition or J&A.

labs.title: Situation to the correct instrument
labs.intro: Match each situation with the right action or document.
pairs: Exercising a priced option on time with funds available
Unilateral modification by the CO
Negotiated equitable adjustment agreed by both parties
Bilateral supplemental agreement
Contractor repeatedly misses deadlines on a curable failure
Cure notice before any default termination
Agency's need ends for budget reasons
Termination for convenience with settlement
Monitoring PWS standards by random sampling
Quality assurance surveillance plan
All work delivered, final payment made
Closeout under FAR 4.804
labs.tip: Know which actions the CO can take alone and which need the contractor's signature.

plaibox.title: Simulation: trouble in performance
plaibox.intro: You are the CO; your COR monitors a janitorial and grounds contract. Score: 2 = best, 1 = partial, 0 = risky.
plaibox.win: Excellent administration: authority respected, records kept, and the contractor treated fairly.
plaibox.lose: Review COR limits, constructive changes, options and cure notices, then try again.

steps.s: The COR asks the contractor to also clean a newly leased annex 'since they're already on site'.
o: Tell the COR to stop and assess it as a possible change
Right — CORs cannot change scope; informal direction creates constructive changes.
Let it run; the annex is small and within scope spirit
Accepting informal direction exposes the agency to claims.
Ask the contractor to track the extra hours for later
Tracking helps, but authority and scope must be settled first.

steps.s: Surveillance shows restrooms failing the PWS standard in 4 of 10 random checks for two months.
o: Withhold all payment immediately until it improves
Unilateral withholding without process invites a dispute.
Issue a documented notice citing the QASP findings
Correct — contemporaneous evidence plus formal notice protects the government.
Mention it informally at the next progress meeting
Talking helps, but undocumented issues are hard to act on later.

steps.s: The option year must be exercised in 10 days; performance has recovered and funds are available.
o: Exercise the option after confirming need, price and terms
Matches FAR 17.207: within terms and time, funds available, most advantageous.
Let it lapse and re-compete for leverage
Possible, but risks a service gap without analysis.
Ask the contractor to keep working while you decide
Directing work beyond the period without a modification creates exposure.

steps.s: The contractor submits a $140,000 claim for the annex work, uncertified.
o: Issue a final decision on the claim as received
A claim over $100,000 needs certification before a valid final decision.
Return it, asking for the required certification
Correct — CDA claims over $100,000 must be certified.
Pay it to avoid a costly dispute later
Paying an unvalidated claim without analysis or authority is improper.

modules.t: Day 3B — AI in Acquisition, Audit-Readiness & Capstone
modules.d: Using AI responsibly across the acquisition lifecycle, building audit-ready files, and your capstone.
modules.body:
AI in federal acquisition

The OECD, the World Bank and U.S. federal policymakers identify procurement as one of the most promising applications of AI in government — and one of the most sensitive for integrity. Federal policy issued in 2025 by the Office of Management and Budget (including memoranda on agencies' use and acquisition of AI) directs agencies to accelerate responsible AI adoption, manage risks for high-impact uses, and strengthen how they buy AI. Agencies are also building AI tools for acquisition workforce tasks. Use agency-approved tools only, and follow current OMB and agency guidance.

Where AI helps across the lifecycle

  • Requirements: drafting and reviewing PWS and SOO language for clarity, measurability and restrictive wording.
  • Market research: summarising capability statements, RFI responses and public information; identifying potential sources.
  • Solicitation: checking alignment between sections C, L and M; generating compliance matrices; drafting standard sections from templates.
  • Evaluation support: organising proposal content against criteria and checking evaluator narratives for consistency and documentation gaps.
  • Contract administration: summarising correspondence, tracking deliverables and deadlines, drafting letters and modification documents.
  • Knowledge work: explaining regulations, but always verified against current FAR and agency text.
Hard lines in acquisition. ① Source selection information and proprietary proposal data go only into tools specifically approved for that sensitivity — never public tools. ② AI must not make or determine award decisions, ratings or responsibility findings; humans with authority decide and document their reasoning. ③ AI-generated regulatory citations must be verified in the current FAR, RFO deviation text and agency supplements. ④ AI outputs used in the record are reviewed and owned by the responsible official.

Buying AI

When the government acquires AI systems, additional considerations apply: clear performance requirements and testing, data rights and ownership, protection of government data (including whether vendors may train on it), transparency and documentation, monitoring for drift and bias, security, avoiding vendor lock-in, and, for high-impact uses, risk management practices required by current federal policy. Performance-based requirements and staged, modular contracting help manage uncertainty.

Audit-readiness

Inspectors General, GAO and agency reviewers examine acquisition files. An audit-ready file (FAR 4.803 lists typical contents) tells the story of the acquisition: requirement and funding documents, acquisition plan, market research, J&As or set-aside decisions, IGCE, solicitation and amendments, proposals, evaluation records, competitive range and discussion records, price analysis, responsibility determination, award decision, debriefings, protests, modifications, surveillance records, performance evaluations, payments and closeout. Common findings include missing documents, unsupported price reasonableness determinations, inadequate trade-off documentation, unauthorized commitments, weak surveillance and late closeout.

Building an integrity culture

Strong acquisition organisations combine clear procedures with training, independent reviews, segregation of duties, ethics awareness, and leadership that supports contracting officers who say "no" to improper requests. Technology, including AI, should strengthen those controls, not bypass them.

Your capstone

Choose a realistic requirement from your environment. Produce: (1) a requirement summary and PWS or SOO extract with measurable standards; (2) a market research summary and set-aside decision; (3) a recommended method and contract type with justification; (4) aligned section L and M outlines; (5) a source selection plan with evaluation factors and trade-off approach; (6) a contract administration plan with QASP outline; (7) an AI-use statement describing approved tools, safeguards and human decision points; and (8) an audit-readiness checklist. Your instructor reviews it as a contracting officer and an auditor would.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my acquisition capstone reviewer, playing both an experienced contracting officer and an Inspector General auditor. I will paste my capstone package. Review each of the eight components for compliance with FAR principles, consistency between requirement, evaluation and administration, and documentation quality. Identify the top ten audit or protest risks, and remind me which current FAR, RFO deviation text, OMB guidance and agency rules I must verify.

📚 Glossary

  • Source selection information: protected information about the evaluation, not to be disclosed before award
  • Contract file: official record of the acquisition (FAR 4.803)
  • High-impact AI use: AI use with significant effects on rights or safety under federal policy
  • Modular contracting: acquiring systems in smaller, successive increments

📖 References

  • OMB memoranda on federal AI use and acquisition (2025) — whitehouse.gov/omb (verify current versions).
  • FAR 4.803 (contract file contents); FAR 3.104 (procurement integrity).
  • OECD — Recommendation on Public Procurement; OECD work on AI in public procurement.
  • GAO and agency Inspector General acquisition audit reports.

quiz.q: A contract specialist wants to paste an offeror's proprietary technical proposal into a public AI chatbot to summarise it. What should she do instead?
opts: Use only a tool approved for that data sensitivity, or summarise it herself
Remove the company name from the text before pasting it into the chatbot as well as its address
Use the chatbot but delete the conversation history after the summary
Ask the offeror for permission to use the public chatbot first
quiz.x: Proprietary and source selection data go only into tools approved for that sensitivity. Removing names or deleting history does not prevent disclosure.

quiz.q: An agency's AI tool ranks proposals and recommends an award. The SSA plans to sign the recommendation without further review. What is wrong?
opts: The AI's ranking must be published to offerors before award
The SSA should also ask a second AI tool to confirm the ranking
Nothing, if the AI tool was approved by the agency's chief information officer for evaluation use
Humans with authority must make and document the decision; AI cannot determine award
quiz.x: AI must not make or determine award decisions or ratings; authorised humans decide and document reasoning. Approval of the tool does not shift decision authority.

quiz.q: An AI assistant drafts a memo citing 'FAR 15.406-9' for a requirement. The specialist cannot find that section. What should she do?
opts: Verify every AI citation against current FAR and RFO deviation text before use
Replace it with a citation to FAR Part 15 generally to avoid errors
Ask the AI tool to confirm the citation and accept its answer
Keep the citation, since AI tools are trained on official regulations using its built-in checker
quiz.x: AI-generated citations must be verified in current FAR and deviation text; AI can hallucinate references, and asking the same tool to confirm is not verification.

quiz.q: A US agency's acquisition team wants to use AI to check alignment between sections C, L and M of a draft RFP. Is this a suitable use?
opts: Yes, and the AI's output can be issued without review since it is advisory to the drafting team
Yes, it is a supporting task, with human review of findings before finalising
No, AI may not be used on any part of a solicitation document
No, because sections C, L and M contain source selection information
quiz.x: Alignment checks are a listed AI support use; humans review outputs. Draft solicitations are not necessarily source selection information requiring a ban.

quiz.q: An auditor asks for the file supporting a $1.2 million award. Which feature would most improve audit readiness?
opts: Email folders containing all correspondence, organised by date with no index
A checklist confirming that each step happened, without supporting documents
A short summary memo prepared after the audit request is received with key dates highlighted and signed by the CO
A complete file showing requirement, market research, competition, evaluation and award rationale
quiz.x: Audit-ready files show the decisions and evidence across the lifecycle. Post-hoc memos and unsupported checklists are weak substitutes.

quiz.q: A program office in Lagos funded by a US grant asks whether AI can be used to draft PWS language. What advice fits the course?
opts: No, PWS documents must be written fully by humans under federal policy
No, because AI tools cannot be used for any procurement documents
Yes, AI can draft and review PWS language, with human verification of accuracy
Yes, and the AI draft can be issued directly if it uses plain language for local partners
quiz.x: Requirements drafting is a listed AI use, with human verification. Blanket bans or unreviewed issuance both contradict the course guidance.

quiz.q: In October 2026 a team asks which source should govern their use of AI in acquisitions. What is the best answer?
opts: The 2023 executive order alone, which remains the sole governing policy
No guidance applies, because AI policy is still in proposed form
Current OMB and agency guidance, checked for updates, plus agency-approved tools
Commercial AI vendors' terms of service, since they define acceptable use for every federal buyer
quiz.x: The lesson points to 2025 OMB memoranda and agency guidance, which change; check current guidance and use approved tools.

quiz.q: A capstone team designs a lifecycle plan for a $3 million services buy. Which element best demonstrates integration of the course modules?
opts: Focusing mainly on AI tools for each phase, since they now drive the process
Describing the award decision alone, since that is what auditors review
Choosing the cheapest contract type and leaving other decisions to evaluation which the course stresses
Linking requirement, market research, method, evaluation and administration decisions
quiz.x: The capstone integrates lifecycle decisions; each choice should follow from the previous ones. Focusing on one phase or tool misses the integration.

quiz.q: An AI tool reviewing evaluator narratives flags that two evaluators described the same weakness differently. What should the team do?
opts: Accept the AI's suggested rewording automatically to save time on the record
Review the flagged narratives and reconcile them with documented reasoning
Remove one evaluator's narrative so the record looks consistent
Set aside the flag, since evaluators may use different wording
quiz.x: AI can flag inconsistencies, but humans reconcile and document. Automatic acceptance or deleting records undermines integrity.

quiz.q: An agency is buying an AI system for a high-impact use, such as screening benefit claims. What should the acquisition emphasise?
opts: Risk management, testing, documentation and rights to monitor performance
Vendor marketing claims, as testing is the vendor's responsibility
Speed of delivery, since OMB requires AI to be acquired within 90 days
The lowest price, since AI products are commercial and interchangeable across agencies
quiz.x: OMB 2025 guidance stresses managing risks for high-impact uses and strengthening how agencies buy AI, including testing and monitoring rights.

facts.t: The FAR section listing typical contract file contents.
facts.more: An audit-ready file tells the acquisition's story from requirement to closeout. Missing documents and unsupported price reasonableness are among the most common findings.

facts.t: Hard lines for AI in acquisition set out in this module.
facts.more: Sensitive data only in approved tools; AI never decides awards, ratings or responsibility; verify every citation; officials own any AI output used in the record.

facts.t: Year OMB issued memoranda on federal agencies' use and acquisition of AI.
facts.more: They push responsible adoption and set risk practices for high-impact uses. Guidance changes — verify the current versions on whitehouse.gov/omb before relying on them.

facts.t: Cycle for statutory inflation adjustment of acquisition thresholds.
facts.more: The latest took effect 1 October 2025. AI tools trained earlier may quote old values such as a $250,000 SAT — a typical error to catch.

labs.title: Where can AI help — and where not?
labs.intro: Sort each use against the module's hard lines.
buckets: Fine with an approved general tool
Only in a tool approved for sensitive data
items: Checking a draft PWS for vague or restrictive wording
Summarising public RFI responses already released
Organising proprietary proposal volumes against Section M
Checking evaluator narratives for consistency during source selection
Deciding which offeror receives award
Making the responsibility determination
Drafting a routine letter acknowledging a deliverable
Assigning technical ratings to proposals
labs.tip: Sensitivity of data decides the tool; authority decides who makes the call — always a human.

labs.title: Spot the problems in this AI-assisted memo
labs.intro: A specialist used a chatbot to draft a price-reasonableness memo. Tap what should not go into the file unchecked.
segments: Three offers were received under the competitive solicitation.
I pasted all three proposals into a free public chatbot to compare prices.
Proprietary proposal data and source selection information may go only into tools approved for that sensitivity.
The AI determined that Offeror B should receive award.
AI must not make award decisions; a warranted official decides and documents the reasoning.
Prices ranged from $280,000 to $315,000, against an IGCE of $300,000.
As the value is above the $250,000 simplified acquisition threshold, full Part 15 procedures apply.
Outdated: the SAT is $350,000 from 1 Oct 2025 — verify AI-generated figures and citations.
Adequate price competition supports a fair and reasonable determination.
Per FAR 15.999-2, no further analysis is needed.
Likely hallucinated citation — every AI citation must be checked in the current FAR and RFO text.
The contracting officer reviewed and signs this memo.
labs.tip: Data sensitivity, human decisions, current thresholds and real citations — check all four.
